why.correct: Albumin makes up about 55–60% of plasma protein. It is made by the liver.
options: Fibrinogen is the smallest of the three main groups, about 4–7% of plasma protein.
Correct. Albumin is more than half of all plasma protein.
Gamma globulins are one part of the globulins, which together make up about 35–38%.
Beta globulins are another part of the globulins, and they are far less abundant than albumin.

why.correct: The liver makes albumin, and albumin supplies most of the plasma's osmotic pull. It stays in the capillaries, so water is drawn toward it. With less albumin, the pull weakens, more water leaves the blood, and the tissues swell.
options: Fibrinogen is made by the liver too, and a failing liver can lower it, but a low fibrinogen causes bleeding. Fluid leaving the blood as clear fluid is set by osmotic pull, and fibrinogen is too scarce to supply much of that.
Gamma globulins are made by white blood cells, not the liver, and swollen ankles from liver disease are not caused by infection.
Correct. Low albumin weakens the osmotic pull that keeps water in the blood.
Hormone carriers do not set how much water stays in the blood, and hormone delivery does not explain swelling.

why.correct: In the middle tube the packed red column fills a much smaller fraction of the tube, and the plasma fills more. Red cells make up less of the blood's volume: the hematocrit is lower than normal.
options: The plasma in both tubes is the same straw color. The difference is in how much of each tube it fills.
Correct. A shorter red column means a lower hematocrit.
The buffy coat is a thin band in both tubes, well under a tenth of the height.
That describes the right tube, where the red column is taller than normal. In the middle tube it is shorter.

why.correct: Hematocrit = red column ÷ whole column × 100% = 20 ÷ 50 × 100% = 40%.
options: 20 is the height of the red column in millimeters, not a percentage of the whole.
30 is the height of the plasma layer (50 − 20), not a percentage.
Correct. 20 ÷ 50 = 0.40, which is 40%.
60% is the share of plasma (30 ÷ 50). The hematocrit is the share of red cells.

why.correct: Red cells are 40% of 4.0 L = 1.6 L. The rest, 4.0 − 1.6 = 2.4 L, is plasma (the buffy coat is too small to matter).
options: 1.6 L is her red cell volume, 40% of her blood.
2.0 L would be half her blood. At a hematocrit of 40%, plasma is 60%, not 50%.
4.0 L is her whole blood volume, cells and plasma together.
Correct. 60% of 4.0 L is 2.4 L of plasma.

why.correct: Losing plasma water leaves the cells and proteins in a smaller volume. Every concentration and ratio that has red cells or proteins on top rises, including the hematocrit, even though the body has not made a single extra red blood cell.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Sweat is made from water drawn out of the plasma, so plasma volume shrinks.

variables.name: Red blood cell volume
variables.why: No red cells leave the body in sweat, and new ones take days to make, so the red cell volume is unchanged.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: The same red cell volume now sits in a smaller total blood volume, so red cells are a larger fraction of it.

variables.name: Plasma protein concentration
variables.why: The proteins stay in the blood while water leaves, so the same amount of protein is dissolved in less water.

variables.name: Blood viscosity
variables.why: Viscosity depends mostly on the hematocrit, which has risen, so the blood is thicker.

why.correct: The buffy coat is the thin, pale band between the plasma and the packed red cells. It holds the white blood cells and platelets, less than 1% of the sample.
options: Correct. White blood cells and platelets settle between the lighter plasma and the denser red cells.
The top layer is plasma, the fluid part of blood, not the buffy coat.
The packed red cells are the bottom layer, whose height gives the hematocrit.
Fat can make plasma cloudy after a fatty meal, but the buffy coat is a layer of cells.

why.correct: Platelets come from the myeloid branch. A myeloid stem cell, driven by thrombopoietin, becomes a giant megakaryocyte, which copies its DNA without dividing. The megakaryocyte reaches into a marrow vessel, and the blood breaks its extensions into thousands of platelets.
The first tube gives serum; the second gives plasma. Serum is plasma without its clotting proteins, because they were used up building the clot. Fibrinogen is the main one.
options: Albumin does not take part in clotting, so it is present in both serum and plasma.
Alpha globulins are transport proteins, and they stay in serum.
Correct. Fibrinogen is turned into the threads of the clot, so serum has none.
Gamma globulins are immune proteins. They remain in serum, which is why many immune tests use serum.

why.correct: Formed elements are the cells and cell fragments of blood: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Proteins and dissolved molecules belong to the plasma.
options: Correct. Platelets are cell fragments, which is why the group is called formed elements rather than cells.
Albumin is a plasma protein, dissolved in the fluid part of blood.
Correct. White blood cells are formed elements.
Correct. Red blood cells are by far the most numerous formed element.
Fibrinogen is a plasma protein, not a cell or fragment.
Glucose is a nutrient dissolved in plasma.

why.correct: Hematocrit is red cell volume divided by total blood volume. Dehydration had shrunk her plasma, raising the ratio. The drip restored plasma volume, so the same red cells became a smaller share of a larger total.
options: Red blood cells circulate for about 120 days, so slowing production for a few hours would barely change their number.
A salt solution given in the right concentration does not burst red blood cells. Her red cell volume is unchanged.
Correct. The denominator of the ratio grew; the numerator stayed the same.
The kidneys filter plasma, not whole cells. They do not remove red blood cells from the blood.

why.correct: Most of blood's viscosity comes from its red cells. A hematocrit of 60% makes blood thicker, and viscosity is one of the factors that set resistance: more viscous blood meets more resistance.
options: Carrying more oxygen does not lower resistance. Resistance depends on viscosity and vessel size, and viscosity has risen.
Correct. Higher hematocrit, higher viscosity, higher resistance.
Plasma proteins add a little to viscosity, but red cells contribute most of it.
More cells rub against each other and the vessel walls more, not less. Crowded cells raise viscosity.

why.correct: In adults, red marrow is found in the flat bones of the trunk and skull (sternum, ribs, vertebrae, hip bones, skull) and in the upper ends of the femur and humerus.
options: The shafts of long bones hold yellow, fatty marrow in adults.
The small bones of the hands and feet hold mostly yellow marrow in adults.
Correct. The sternum is a flat bone full of red marrow, which is why marrow samples are sometimes taken from it.
The radius shaft, like other limb-bone shafts, holds yellow marrow in adults.

why.correct: Colony-stimulating factors drive marrow precursors to make white blood cells. Given as a drug after chemotherapy, one speeds the recovery of the white cell count.
options: Erythropoietin speeds red blood cell production, not white.
Thrombopoietin drives megakaryocytes and platelet production.
Albumin is a plasma protein that holds water in the blood. It is not a growth factor.
Correct. Colony-stimulating factors steer marrow cells toward white blood cells.

why.correct: The hematopoietic stem cell's daughters commit to one of two branches: the myeloid branch or the lymphoid branch. Lymphoid stem cells give rise to the immune system's central family of white blood cells.
options: Correct. The lymphoid stem cell is the other branch.
A megakaryocyte is a late cell on the myeloid branch that sheds platelets.
Red blood cells come from the myeloid branch, not a separate branch of their own.
Mesenchymal cells are embryonic connective tissue cells, not a branch of blood cell production.

why.correct: Serum is the fluid left after clotting. Its fibrinogen was used up building the clot, so serum has little or none. Fluid that still contains fibrinogen would be plasma.
options: This step is right. Serum needs blood that is allowed to clot.
This step is right. Blood in a plain tube clots within about half an hour.
This step is right. Clotting turns fibrinogen into insoluble threads that trap the cells.
This is the error. Serum lacks fibrinogen; the clot consumed it.

why.correct: Blood is always red. Red blood cells full of oxygen make it bright scarlet; with less oxygen it is dark red. Veins look blue through skin because skin scatters and absorbs red and blue light differently, not because the blood is blue.
options: Blood drawn into a sealed tube, never meeting air, is still dark red. It is not blue inside the body.
Correct. The color of a vein seen through skin is an effect of light in the skin.
Carbon dioxide does not turn blood purple. Blood with less oxygen is darker red.
Blood in the limbs and the core is the same color for the same oxygen content. Blood is never blue.

why.correct: Blood regulates pH through its buffers, body temperature by carrying heat, and fluid balance through the osmotic pull of its proteins.
options: Correct. Bicarbonate, phosphate and proteins buffer blood pH within 7.35–7.45.
Correct. Blood picks up heat in warm tissues and loses it where skin vessels are widened.
Blood carries hormones; glands make them. Plasma itself makes no hormones.
Correct. Albumin held in the capillaries draws water toward the blood.
Mature red blood cells cannot divide. New ones come from the marrow.

why.correct: Thrombopoietin is made mainly by the liver and drives megakaryocytes to make platelets. A failing liver makes less of it, so platelet counts can fall.
options: Erythropoietin comes from the kidneys, not the liver.
Correct. Less thrombopoietin, fewer platelets.
Colony-stimulating factors are made by white blood cells, vessel lining cells and marrow fibroblasts, not mainly by the liver.
Thrombopoietin does come mainly from the liver, but it drives platelet production, not red cell production.

why.correct: Without mitochondria, a red cell cannot use oxygen to make ATP. It splits glucose by glycolysis, which needs no oxygen, so none of the oxygen it carries is used up on the way.
options: Correct. Glycolysis runs in the cytosol and needs no mitochondria.
Using oxygen to make ATP happens in mitochondria, which mature red cells have lost.
ATP cannot be stored for 120 days. The cell must keep making it to run its ion pumps.
Hemoglobin is not broken down until the cell dies. The cell's fuel is glucose from the plasma.

why.correct: Each hemoglobin has four hemes, each with one iron that binds one oxygen molecule: 250 million × 4 = 1,000 million, or 1 billion.
options: That counts one oxygen per hemoglobin. Each molecule carries four.
That counts two per hemoglobin, one for each pair of chains. Every chain has its own heme.
Correct. Four oxygen molecules per hemoglobin.
That multiplies by 16. Each hemoglobin has four hemes, not sixteen.

why.correct: Thin air lowers the oxygen reaching the kidneys. Through the erythropoiesis feedback loop, EPO rises within hours and the marrow speeds up. EPO eases back from its early peak over the following days, but the extra red cells keep coming for weeks. Her red cell count, hematocrit and hemoglobin climb, and the cost is thicker blood.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count
variables.why: EPO makes more erythroid precursors survive and mature, so more young red cells enter the blood each day.

variables.name: Red blood cell count
variables.why: Weeks of faster production add more red cells than are destroyed.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: The red cell volume has grown, so red cells are a larger share of the blood's volume.

variables.name: Hemoglobin per liter of blood
variables.why: More red cells in each liter means more hemoglobin in each liter.

variables.name: Blood viscosity
variables.why: Viscosity depends mostly on the hematocrit, which has risen.

why.correct: The feedback loop's sensor and signal both sit in the kidney. When the kidneys fail, the stimulus (low oxygen) is present but the signal (EPO) is missing, so the marrow is never told to speed up. The result is anemia with a low reticulocyte count, which is treated by injecting EPO.

variables.name: Erythropoietin release
variables.why: The damaged kidneys have lost many of the cells that make EPO, so less is released even though oxygen delivery is low.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count
variables.why: With little EPO, fewer erythroid precursors survive and mature, so fewer young red cells reach the blood.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: Red cells are still destroyed at the usual rate but replaced more slowly, so their share of the blood falls.

variables.name: Oxygen carried per liter of blood
variables.why: Fewer red cells means less hemoglobin in each liter, so less oxygen is carried.

variables.name: Resting heart rate
variables.why: With thinner blood and less oxygen in each liter, his heart pumps more blood each minute, partly by beating faster.

why.correct: Macrophages break down old red cells, split off the iron and open the heme ring into biliverdin, then bilirubin. Poorly soluble bilirubin rides on albumin to the liver, which conjugates it and secretes it in bile. In the intestine, bacteria later turn it into urobilinogen and then brown stercobilin.
Biliverdin, the green pigment made when the heme ring is opened, is converted into yellow bilirubin. Bilirubin is what the liver conjugates.
options: Correct. Biliverdin becomes bilirubin.
Ferritin stores the iron that was removed from heme. It is not made from the ring.
Transferrin carries iron in the plasma, not the heme ring.
Stercobilin forms later, from bilirubin, in the intestine.

why.correct: Erythropoietin is released mainly by oxygen-sensing cells in the kidneys. The marrow is the effector that responds to it, not the sensor or the source.
options: This step is right. Fewer red cells means less oxygen reaches every tissue, including the kidneys.
This is the error. The kidneys sense low oxygen and release EPO; the marrow responds.
This step is right. EPO acts on precursors in the red marrow.
This step is right. Reticulocytes rise within 3–5 days.
This step is right. The response removes the stimulus: negative feedback.

why.correct: Each heavy period removes iron in the lost red cells. Over months her stores run out, which a low plasma ferritin shows. Without iron, erythroblasts cannot fill with hemoglobin, so the cells come out small and pale.
options: A lack of B12 stalls DNA synthesis, so red cells come out large, not small, and ferritin is normal.
Kidney failure lowers EPO, but the cells it produces are normal in size and iron stores are normal.
Correct. Small, pale cells with empty iron stores point to iron deficiency.
Early destruction raises the reticulocyte count and the bilirubin, and the body keeps the recovered iron, so ferritin would not be low.

why.correct: Absorbing vitamin B12 in the intestine needs a carrier protein made by cells of the stomach lining. With those cells destroyed, swallowed B12 passes through unabsorbed. An injection puts B12 straight into the body, bypassing absorption. (Very high oral doses can also work, because about 1% of swallowed B12 is absorbed without the carrier.)
options: Correct. This is pernicious anemia: the problem is absorption, not intake.
B12 survives stomach acid. The problem is the missing carrier protein needed to absorb it further along.
Injected B12 goes into muscle and reaches the marrow through the blood like any nutrient. It does not need to be delivered into bone.
His large cells point to a lack of B12, not iron. B12 contains no iron.

why.correct: A high reticulocyte count shows a healthy marrow working hard, so the red cells are being lost, not underproduced. Jaundice shows that heme is being broken down faster than the liver can clear bilirubin. Together they point to hemolysis, early destruction of red cells.
options: In aplastic anemia the marrow has failed, so the reticulocyte count is very low.
Correct. Fast destruction explains both the jaundice and the busy marrow.
Without iron, the marrow cannot respond, so reticulocytes stay low and ferritin is low.
With too little EPO, the marrow is not driven to respond, so reticulocytes stay low, and there is no extra bilirubin.

why.correct: Pale feces mean no bilirubin is reaching the intestine to become brown stercobilin. Dark urine means conjugated bilirubin, the water-soluble kind, is backing up into the blood and spilling into the urine. Both fit a blockage after the liver, such as a gallstone.
options: Fast breakdown raises mostly unconjugated bilirubin, which cannot enter urine, and more pigment reaches the gut, not less. Feces would not be pale.
If the liver could not take up bilirubin, the excess would be unconjugated, which does not darken urine.
Correct. A blocked outflow sends conjugated bilirubin back into the blood.
Urobilin is a small share of pigment and does not cause jaundice. Less of it would make urine paler, not darker.

why.correct: Ferritin stores iron inside liver cells, macrophages and marrow. A small amount leaks into plasma in proportion to the stores, so a low plasma ferritin means the stores are empty.
options: Transferrin carries iron in transit between gut, stores and marrow. It does not measure the stores themselves.
Correct. Plasma ferritin tracks iron stores.
Hemoglobin falls only after the stores are exhausted, so it is a late sign.
The reticulocyte count shows how fast the marrow is working, not how much iron is stored.

why.correct: HbS forms fibers when it has given up its oxygen, and it does so faster the more concentrated it is. Low oxygen makes more HbS unload; dehydration shrinks the cell and concentrates the HbS. Stiff sickled cells then jam small vessels.
options: New red cells take days to make, and a crisis starts within hours. Fiber formation, not new cells, is the trigger.
The spleen does not store and release sickle cells. It is damaged by them.
The problem is the opposite: sickling happens after HbS has let go of its oxygen.
Correct. Less oxygen bound and a more crowded cell both speed fiber formation.

why.correct: Each parent passes on either the sickle gene or the normal gene, with equal chance. The child has the disease only with two sickle genes: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
options: Each parent carries a sickle gene, so a child can inherit one from each.
Correct. One in four children would inherit two sickle genes.
One in two is the chance that a child has the trait (one sickle gene), not the disease.
A child gets the disease only with a sickle gene from both parents, which happens in about a quarter of children.

why.correct: In polycythemia vera, mutant stem cells make red cells without waiting for EPO; the high red cell count delivers plenty of oxygen to the kidneys, so EPO is low. With lung disease, low oxygen drives the kidneys to release more EPO, and the marrow responds normally.
options: With the same hematocrit, viscosity is about the same in both men.
With the same hematocrit, hemoglobin is about the same in both.
Correct. EPO separates primary polycythemia from secondary.
The marrow in polycythemia vera is making red cells fast, so reticulocytes are present.

why.correct: Altitude and lung disease lower the oxygen reaching the kidneys, which release more EPO. A tumor or doping adds EPO directly. Dehydration and a marrow mutation raise the red cell count or hematocrit without raising EPO.
options: Correct. Thin air lowers oxygen delivery to the kidneys.
Dehydration raises the hematocrit by shrinking the plasma. The red cell count is unchanged and EPO does not rise.
Correct. Poorly working lungs load less oxygen into the blood.
Correct. The tumor bypasses the feedback loop.
This is polycythemia vera: red cells rise without EPO, and EPO falls.
Correct. Injected EPO acts on the marrow like the body's own.

why.correct: Polycythemia means too many red blood cells, so the packed red column fills more of the tube: a high hematocrit, as in the right tube.
options: The left tube shows a normal hematocrit.
The middle tube shows a low hematocrit, as in anemia.
Correct. A tall red column is a high hematocrit.
Extra red cells take up more of the sample's volume, so the column is visibly taller.

why.correct: Each globin chain holds one heme: a flat ring with an iron ion at its center, where one oxygen molecule binds.
options: Globin is the folded protein chain that holds the heme, not the flat ring itself.
Correct. The flat, iron-holding ring is heme.
Ferritin is an iron-storage protein inside cells, not part of hemoglobin.
Transferrin carries iron in the plasma; it is not part of hemoglobin.

why.correct: A red blood cell lasts about 120 days. It cannot make new proteins, so it wears out and is removed by macrophages.
options: 7 to 10 days is the lifespan of a platelet.
Correct. About four months.
A red cell with no nucleus cannot repair itself for that long.
Some white blood cells live for years, but red cells do not.

why.correct: A wound loses whole blood, cells and plasma in the same proportion, so the hematocrit is unchanged at first. Over the next hours, fluid moves into the blood from the tissues and dilutes the remaining cells, and the hematocrit falls. A normal early hematocrit does not rule out a large bleed.
options: The hematocrit is a ratio; it cannot show a loss of volume in the first minutes.
Making red cells takes days, and reticulocytes rise only after 3–5 days.
The value is expected. The fall comes later, as plasma is refilled.
Correct. The ratio falls only once fluid moves in to refill the plasma.

why.correct: Fetal red cells live only about 60–90 days, and a newborn breaks many of them down at once, making a lot of bilirubin. Its liver's conjugating enzyme is still immature, so bilirubin builds up for a few days.
options: Correct. More bilirubin made, and less cleared.
Before birth, bilirubin crosses to the mother, who clears it. The kidneys are not the main route for bilirubin.
Newborn red cells are full of hemoglobin; that is where the bilirubin comes from.
Newborns do have macrophages, and fetal red cells live shorter lives, not longer.

why.correct: Adult hemoglobin has four globin chains, two alpha and two beta, and each chain holds its own heme with one iron ion.
options: Two chains and two hemes could carry only two oxygen molecules. Hemoglobin carries four.
The four hemes are held by four separate chains, one each.
Correct. Four chains, four hemes, four iron ions.
Every globin chain has its own heme, so there are four.

why.correct: A nucleus of several lobes joined by thin strands, with faint lilac granules, marks a neutrophil.
options: Correct. Three to five lobes and faint granules: a neutrophil.
An eosinophil has a two-lobed nucleus and large red-orange granules.
A basophil is packed with large dark purple granules that hide its nucleus.
A monocyte has a single kidney-shaped nucleus and no visible granules.

why.correct: Large, dark blue-purple granules crowded over the nucleus mark a basophil.
options: A neutrophil's granules are small and faint, and its many-lobed nucleus is easy to see.
A lymphocyte has no visible granules; its large round nucleus almost fills the cell.
An eosinophil's granules are red-orange, and its two lobes are clearly visible.
Correct. Dark granules that hide the nucleus: a basophil.

why.correct: Neutrophils make up about 50–70% of white blood cells.
options: Lymphocytes are second, at about 20–40%.
Monocytes are only about 2–8%.
Correct. Neutrophils are the most common.
Eosinophils are about 1–4%.

why.correct: Eosinophils attack parasitic worms, which are too large to engulf, by releasing toxic granule proteins onto their surface. Worm infections raise the eosinophil count.
options: Basophils rarely rise, and they are not the main defense against worms.
Correct. Parasitic worms drive eosinophilia.
Neutrophils rise mainly in bacterial infections.
Monocytes rise in long-lasting infections, not typically in worm infections.

why.correct: Lymphocytes are the cells of specific immunity, and viral infections typically raise their numbers. Infectious mononucleosis, caused by a virus, is a classic example.
options: Worm infections raise eosinophils, not lymphocytes.
Bacterial infections typically raise neutrophils.
Allergic reactions raise eosinophils.
Correct. A rise in lymphocytes points to a viral infection.

why.correct: Absolute count = total × fraction = 1,500 × 0.30 = 450 per µL. That is below 500, so her risk of serious bacterial infection is very high.
options: 30 is the percentage, not a count.
4,500 comes from multiplying by 3 instead of 0.30.
Correct. 1,500 × 0.30 = 450 neutrophils per µL.
1,050 is the count of all the other white cells (70% of 1,500).

why.correct: 20,000 × 0.08 = 1,600 lymphocytes per µL, which is within the normal absolute range. The percentage fell only because neutrophils rose so much. Always convert to absolute counts before calling a type high or low.
options: The percentage is low, but the absolute number is normal. Percentages shift whenever another type rises.
Correct. The absolute lymphocyte count is normal.
A high total does not raise every type. Here the rise is almost all neutrophils.
Multiplying the differential percentage by the total gives each type's absolute count, so it can be judged.

why.correct: In acute leukemia, one precursor multiplies without maturing. The blasts fill the blood but do not work, and by crowding the marrow they stop normal hematopoiesis, so he has few working neutrophils. The same crowding explains his anemia and low platelets.
options: Correct. Many cells, few that work.
White cells do not fail from a hemoglobin of 7; the problem is that normal white cells are not being made.
Antibodies are not used up by white cell numbers.
Low platelets cause bruising and bleeding, not infections.

why.correct: Lymphoma is cancer of lymphocytes that grows mainly as solid tumors in lymph nodes, often with a normal blood count.
options: Leukemias start in the marrow and usually change the blood count; myeloid leukemias come from the other branch.
Correct. Cancerous lymphocytes growing in lymph nodes is lymphoma.
Mononucleosis causes swollen nodes, but it is a viral infection, and a biopsy would not show cancer.
Chronic myeloid leukemia comes from the myeloid branch and raises the white count.

why.correct: Every leukocyte keeps its nucleus, can squeeze out of the blood into tissue, and descends from hematopoietic stem cells. Only granulocytes have visible granules, and no leukocyte carries hemoglobin.
options: Correct. Unlike mature red cells, leukocytes keep their nucleus.
Correct. They do most of their work in the tissues.
Only the three granulocytes have visible granules; lymphocytes and monocytes do not.
Correct. Both branches of hematopoiesis start from the same stem cell.
Hemoglobin is carried by red blood cells, not leukocytes.

why.correct: Signals from the injury make the local capillary lining sticky. Neutrophils stick, squeeze out through the wall, follow the signals through the tissue and engulf the bacteria, killing them with their granules and toxic oxygen compounds.
Monocytes circulate for a day to three, then leave the blood and mature into macrophages, long-lived phagocytes that clear bacteria, dead cells and debris.
options: Neutrophils are a separate granulocyte line; monocytes do not turn into them.
Lymphocytes come from the lymphoid branch, not from monocytes.
Mast cells are tissue cells with histamine granules, from a different precursor.
Correct. A monocyte in the tissues becomes a macrophage.

why.correct: An antigen is a molecule that the immune system recognizes as a specific target. Proteins and glycoproteins on a microbe's surface are typical antigens.
options: That is an antibody, which binds an antigen.
Correct. The recognized surface molecule is the antigen.
A digestive enzyme is part of the neutrophil's killing machinery, not a recognized target.
A lysosome is an organelle, not a molecule recognized as a target.

why.correct: An antibody's arms each bind the same antigen. If one arm binds a bacterium and another binds a second bacterium, the two are linked. Many such links build clumps.
options: Correct. Two or more binding sites let one antibody bridge two cells.
Antibodies bind; they do not dissolve cell walls by themselves.
Antibodies are highly specific: each binds only one antigen shape.
Antibodies do not make bacteria divide.

why.correct: Aging platelets change their surface, and macrophages, mainly in the spleen and liver, recognize and engulf them. The marrow replaces them with new platelets from megakaryocytes.
options: Platelets are far too large to pass the kidney's filter. They are removed whole by phagocytes.
A platelet has no nucleus and cannot divide.
Correct. Macrophages in the spleen and liver clear old platelets.
Platelets do not go back to the marrow. New ones are shed by megakaryocytes, and old ones are engulfed.

why.correct: Normally about a third of the platelets are held in the spleen. An enlarged spleen holds many more, so fewer circulate, even though the marrow makes a normal number.
options: Thrombopoietin comes mainly from the liver, and more of it would raise the count, not lower it.
Correct. The platelets are pooled in the spleen, not missing from the body.
Megakaryocytes stay in the marrow; they do not migrate to the spleen.
Platelets are fragments and cannot become red cells.

why.correct: Monocytes come from the myeloid branch, through their own precursor, the monoblast. Although they lack visible granules, they are not on the lymphoid branch.
options: The lymphoid branch leads only to lymphocytes.
The myeloblast gives rise to the three granulocytes.
Correct. Myeloid stem cell, then monoblast, then monocyte.
The megakaryoblast leads to megakaryocytes and platelets.

why.correct: The three granulocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils, all come from the myeloblast.
options: The monoblast leads to monocytes.
The lymphoblast is on the lymphoid branch and leads to lymphocytes.
Correct. The myeloblast gives rise to the granulocytes.
The megakaryoblast leads to megakaryocytes and platelets.

why.correct: A megakaryocyte copies its DNA many times without dividing, which is why it grows so large. Platelets are fragments of its cytoplasm, not daughter cells from mitosis, and they have no nucleus.
options: This step is right. Thrombopoietin, made mainly by the liver, drives the megakaryocyte line.
This step is right. The megakaryoblast is the precursor.
This is the error. Platelets are fragments, not the products of cell division.
This step is right. The arms reach into the vessel.
This step is right. The blood pinches the arms into fragments.

why.correct: Chemotherapy stops hematopoiesis for a time. Formed elements with the shortest lives disappear first: neutrophils within days, platelets within a week or two. Red cells last 120 days, so anemia develops more slowly, but the reticulocyte count falls at once.

variables.name: Neutrophil count
variables.why: Neutrophils live only a day or two, so once the marrow stops making them, their count falls within days.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Platelets last 7–10 days, so two weeks without new ones leaves few in the blood.

variables.name: Risk of bacterial infection
variables.why: With few neutrophils, bacteria that enter the body are not engulfed and killed quickly.

variables.name: Tendency to bruise and bleed
variables.why: With few platelets, small breaks in vessel walls are not sealed.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count
variables.why: The marrow's dividing erythroid precursors are killed too, so fewer young red cells are released.

why.correct: The vessel constricts within seconds, a platelet plug builds over the next minute or two, coagulation reinforces it with fibrin over several minutes, and within an hour platelets pull the clot tight. The steps overlap, but they start in this order.

Initiation happens on the tissue factor cell and yields a trickle of thrombin. Amplification: that thrombin primes platelets and cofactors. Propagation: the activated platelet surface makes a burst of thrombin, enough to convert fibrinogen to fibrin, which XIIIa cross-links.

Vitamin K is needed for four clotting factors. Without it, the liver makes non-working copies, clotting tests lengthen (the PT first) and the person bruises and bleeds easily. Platelets are unaffected.

variables.name: Working factors II, VII, IX and X in plasma
variables.why: The liver needs vitamin K to add the calcium-binding groups these factors need. Without it, the factors it makes do not work.

variables.name: Prothrombin time (PT)
variables.why: The PT depends on factor VII and the common pathway factors X and II. Factor VII has the shortest life in plasma, so the PT lengthens first.

variables.name: aPTT
variables.why: The aPTT depends on factor IX and the common pathway factors X and II, all of which need vitamin K.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Vitamin K is needed for clotting factors, not for making platelets.

variables.name: Tendency to bleed
variables.why: With too little working thrombin-making machinery, fibrin forms slowly, and bleeding lasts longer.

why.correct: The PT tests the extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the common pathway. A normal aPTT shows that the intrinsic and common pathways work. The one factor only the PT depends on is factor VII.
options: Factor VIII is in the intrinsic pathway; a lack of it lengthens the aPTT, not the PT.
A lack of factor XII lengthens the aPTT only.
Correct. Factor VII is tested by the PT alone.
Factor IX is in the intrinsic pathway; a lack of it lengthens the aPTT.

why.correct: Bleeding into a joint is the typical pattern of a clotting factor problem. A long aPTT with a normal PT points to the intrinsic pathway, where factors VIII and IX act. The genes for both lie on the X chromosome, which is why the disease runs in males of a family.
options: Correct. Hemophilia A or B.
His platelet count is normal, and low platelets cause skin and mucous membrane bleeding, not joint bleeds.
Vitamin K deficiency lengthens the PT, often before the aPTT, because factor VII is affected.
Von Willebrand disease mainly causes skin and mucous membrane bleeding, such as nosebleeds, rather than joint bleeds.

why.correct: In a test tube, contact with glass activates factor XII, which starts the intrinsic pathway. In the body, bleeding is stopped by clotting that starts when tissue factor is exposed, so factor XII is not needed. This is one of the observations the cell-based model explains and the lab model does not.
options: The aPTT measures the test-tube pathway accurately. The long result is real; it just does not predict bleeding here.
Factor XII is not needed to stop bleeding in any vessel.
Correct. Tissue factor starts clotting in the body.
Factor VIII does not replace factor XII; they act at different steps.

why.correct: Aspirin permanently blocks cyclooxygenase, the enzyme platelets use to make thromboxane A2. A platelet has no nucleus and makes almost no new enzyme. The effect lasts until the affected platelets are replaced, which takes their 7–10 day lifespan.
options: Aspirin itself is cleared from the blood within hours. The effect outlasts the drug.
Correct. The effect lasts as long as the platelets do.
Warfarin works through vitamin K. Aspirin acts on platelets.
Aspirin does not lower the platelet count; it makes the existing platelets work less well.

why.correct: Heparin binds antithrombin and speeds its action about a thousandfold. Antithrombin then inactivates thrombin and factor Xa, so fibrin forms far more slowly.
options: Heparin does not dissolve existing clots; plasmin does that.
Blocking factor production is how warfarin works, and it takes days.
Citrate in blood collection tubes binds calcium. Heparin works through antithrombin.
Correct. Heparin boosts the body's own inhibitor.

why.correct: Warfarin blocks the recycling of vitamin K. Leafy greens bring in fresh vitamin K, which partly overcomes the block, so the liver makes more working factors II, VII, IX and X. Clotting speeds up and the INR falls.
options: Spinach supplies vitamin K; it does not block its recycling.
Vitamin K from food directly affects how many working factors the liver makes.
Correct. Extra vitamin K works against warfarin.
The effect comes from the vitamin K in the spinach, not from destroying warfarin.

why.correct: Warfarin stops the liver from making new working factors II, VII, IX and X, but it does nothing to the working factors already circulating. Those are cleared over days, so the effect builds as they run out. Heparin acts directly on antithrombin in the plasma.
options: Correct. Warfarin cuts supply; the old stock runs down over days.
Warfarin is absorbed within hours; the delay comes after absorption.
Warfarin and heparin are unrelated molecules with different targets.
Warfarin acts on the liver's vitamin K enzyme, not on platelets.

why.correct: Intact lining keeps platelets quiet with nitric oxide and prostacyclin, removes the ADP that recruits them, and uses thrombomodulin to switch thrombin from a clotting enzyme to an activator of protein C, which destroys Va and VIIIa.
options: Correct. Both keep platelets from activating.
Correct. Without ADP, passing platelets are not recruited.
Tissue factor sits on cells outside the lining and starts clotting when a tear exposes it.
Correct. Thrombomodulin turns thrombin into a brake.
Von Willebrand factor on exposed collagen helps platelets adhere; it promotes the plug.

why.correct: Skin and mucous membrane bleeding with a normal platelet count, in several family members, fits von Willebrand disease. Without enough von Willebrand factor, platelets cannot hold on to exposed collagen. The aPTT is slightly long because vWF also carries and protects factor VIII.
options: Vascular spasm does not explain a long aPTT or inherited mucosal bleeding.
Too much fibrinolysis is rare and would not lengthen the aPTT.
Correct. Poor adhesion from too little vWF.
Clot retraction happens after a clot forms; it does not explain these tests.

why.correct: A clot that forms in an unbroken vessel and stays attached is a thrombus. A piece carried along in the blood is an embolus. The blockage it causes where it lodges is an embolism, here a pulmonary embolism.
options: The clot in the calf is attached where it formed, so it is a thrombus, not an embolus.
Correct. Thrombus, embolus, embolism.
The traveling piece is the embolus; the blockage is the embolism.
The calf clot is a thrombus; an embolism is a blockage, not a clot in place.

why.correct: tPA converts plasminogen, which is built into the clot, into the enzyme plasmin. Plasmin cuts fibrin into fragments, dissolving the clot. This is fibrinolysis.
options: Blocking thrombin stops new fibrin forming but does not dissolve a clot.
Correct. tPA drives fibrinolysis.
Platelet activation would help build a clot, not dissolve it.
That is how heparin works; it prevents growth but does not dissolve an existing clot.

why.correct: Plasminogen is the inactive precursor; tPA converts it to plasmin, the enzyme that cuts fibrin.
options: Thrombin makes fibrin; it does not break it down.
Correct. Plasmin dissolves the clot.
Prothrombin is the inactive form of thrombin.
Fibrinogen is the soluble precursor of fibrin, not an enzyme that cuts it.

why.correct: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin from healthy lining keep platelets from activating. Platelets are activated by binding collagen and vWF, and then by ADP, thromboxane A2 and thrombin.
options: This step is right. Exposed collagen starts the plug.
This step is right. vWF bridges collagen to platelets.
This is the error. Those chemicals inhibit platelets; they limit the plug to the injury.
This step is right. ADP and thromboxane A2 recruit more platelets.
This step is right. One fibrinogen molecule can bind two platelets.

why.correct: Thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII and XI, and those speed its own production. The response strengthens the stimulus, which is positive feedback. The loop is ended by sealing the injury and by inhibitors outside it.
options: Correct. More thrombin makes still more thrombin.
Returning a variable to a set point is negative feedback.
Thrombin is made in response to injury, not to high pressure.
Switching off its own production would be negative feedback. The brakes come from the healthy lining and antithrombin.

why.correct: Too few platelets cause bleeding from small vessels in the skin and mucous membranes: petechiae and bleeding gums. A clotting factor problem causes deep bleeding into joints and muscles, and bleeding that restarts hours later, because the platelet plug forms but no fibrin reinforces it.
options: Patient B's platelet count is normal, and his bleeding pattern is the factor pattern.
Patient A's platelet count of 12,000 per µL is severe thrombocytopenia.
The patterns are the other way round.
Correct. Skin and mucosa for platelets; joints and delayed bleeding for factors.

why.correct: Thrombin cuts fibrinogen, a soluble plasma protein, into fibrin, which links up into insoluble threads.
options: Plasminogen becomes plasmin, the enzyme that breaks fibrin down.
Prothrombin is converted into thrombin itself, by factor Xa.
Correct. Fibrinogen becomes fibrin.
Tissue factor is a membrane protein that starts clotting; it is not converted into fibrin.

why.correct: Calcium ions (factor IV) hold clotting factors onto phospholipid surfaces at most steps. Citrate binds calcium, so coagulation cannot proceed until the lab adds calcium back.
options: Citrate leaves platelets intact; the plasma is spun off them.
Correct. No free calcium, no coagulation.
Fibrinogen stays in the plasma; the tests need it.
Vitamin K acts in the liver while factors are made. It has no role in a blood sample.

why.correct: Little vitamin K reaches the fetus, and breast milk is low in it. The newborn gut is only beginning to gain bacteria, and how much they would add is uncertain anyway. Without vitamin K the liver makes non-working factors II, VII, IX and X, and a rare but serious bleeding disease can follow. One injection prevents it.
options: Newborns have normal platelet counts.
Correct. Low stores at birth and little in breast milk.
Vitamin K is given for clotting, not for bilirubin.
Newborn livers make fibrinogen. The problem is the vitamin K–dependent factors.

why.correct: The injured smooth muscle contracts directly, platelets release constricting chemicals, and local pain reflexes add to the constriction.
options: Correct. Damaged smooth muscle contracts.
Correct. Both constrict the vessel.
Correct. Local reflexes add to the spasm.
Plasmin dissolves clots days later; it does not constrict vessels.
Heparin is an anticoagulant; it does not constrict vessels.

why.correct: Type B red cells carry the B antigen, and the plasma holds antibodies against the ABO antigen the cells lack: anti-A.
options: Anti-B would attack the person's own red cells. The immune system does not make antibodies against its own antigens.
A antigens with anti-B antibodies describes type A.
Only type AB plasma lacks ABO antibodies.
Correct. B antigens, anti-A antibodies.

why.correct: Clumping with anti-A and anti-B means the red cells carry both A and B antigens: type AB. No clumping with anti-D means no D antigen: Rh negative.
options: Type O cells carry neither A nor B, so they would not clump with anti-A or anti-B.
Correct. A and B present, D absent.
An Rh-positive sample would clump in the anti-D well too.
Type O cells would stay smooth in all three wells if Rh negative.

why.correct: Her plasma holds anti-A and anti-B, so she can receive only red cells with neither antigen: type O. As an Rh-positive person she makes no anti-D, so either Rh-positive or Rh-negative O cells are safe.
options: Correct. Only type O cells, of either Rh type.
O negative is also safe: it lacks the D antigen, which she already has.
A, B and AB red cells would meet her anti-A or anti-B.
Her anti-A and anti-B would attack A and B red cells whatever their Rh type.

why.correct: An ABO-incompatible transfusion sets off an immediate antibody attack on the donor cells. Agglutination and hemolysis release hemoglobin into the plasma and urine, and the reaction causes fever and a fall in blood pressure. The transfusion must be stopped at once.

variables.name: Agglutination of the donor red cells
variables.why: The patient's anti-B binds the B antigens on the donor cells and cross-links them into clumps.

variables.name: Free hemoglobin in the plasma
variables.why: Antibodies on the donor cells trigger plasma proteins that burst them, releasing hemoglobin into the plasma.

variables.name: Hemoglobin in the urine
variables.why: Free hemoglobin in the plasma is small enough to be filtered by the kidneys and spills into the urine, darkening it.

variables.name: Body temperature
variables.why: Chemical signals released during the antibody attack cause fever and chills.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Signals released in the reaction widen blood vessels, so pressure falls and shock can follow.

why.correct: What matters is whether the recipient's plasma has antibodies against the donor cells' antigens. An AB-positive person already carries A, B and D, so they make antibodies against none of them.
options: Red cells do not bind other red cells. The danger comes from antibodies in the recipient's plasma.
Correct. No anti-A, anti-B or anti-D in the plasma.
Their immune system works normally; it simply makes no antibodies against antigens on its own cells.
Dilution of donor antibodies helps any recipient; it does not explain why AB positive accepts every red cell type.

why.correct: For plasma, the question is which antibodies the donor plasma carries. AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B, so it cannot attack the recipient's red cells, whatever her type. For plasma, AB is the universal donor.
options: Type O plasma holds anti-A and anti-B, which would attack the red cells of an A, B or AB recipient.
Type A plasma holds anti-B, which would attack B or AB red cells.
Type B plasma holds anti-A, which would attack A or AB red cells.
Correct. AB plasma carries no ABO antibodies.

why.correct: He has no anti-D yet, so the donor cells are not attacked at once. Over the next weeks his immune system may make anti-D against the D antigen he has met. A later Rh-positive transfusion could then trigger a reaction.
options: An immediate reaction needs antibodies already present. Anti-D forms only after exposure.
Correct. The first exposure sensitizes; the danger comes later.
Transfused cells live about 120 days at most; his own red cells stay Rh negative.
Rh matters for any future transfusion. In men there is no pregnancy risk, which is why O-positive blood is often used for men in emergencies.

why.correct: Fetal red cells entered her blood at the first delivery, and she made anti-D. That kind of antibody crosses from mother to fetus. In this Rh-positive fetus, it binds and destroys red cells: hemolytic disease of the newborn.
options: The history of a first Rh-positive baby without treatment points to maternal anti-D, not an inherited enzyme defect.
A fetus does not attack its own antigens; the antibodies come from the mother.
The problem here is Rh, not ABO, and most anti-A cannot cross to the fetus.
Correct. Maternal anti-D from the first pregnancy.

why.correct: The bloods of mother and fetus normally stay apart, and most mixing happens at delivery. The mother then makes anti-D over the following weeks, after the baby has been born. The antibodies threaten the next Rh-positive pregnancy.
options: Correct. The timing of the first exposure protects the first baby.
Rh-positive fetuses carry the D antigen well before birth.
Before the first delivery she usually has no anti-D to destroy.
The protection comes from timing, not from extra red cells.

why.correct: The injected anti-D clears the fetal Rh-positive cells that entered her blood at delivery before her immune system responds to them, so she never starts making her own anti-D. The injected antibody is gone within months and does not harm later pregnancies.
options: The injection is for the mother, and it does not protect the baby against infection.
Correct. It prevents her from becoming sensitized.
Nothing changes her own red cells' Rh type.
Anti-D cannot destroy anti-D. Once she has made her own, the injection no longer helps.

why.correct: The mother has two O copies and passes on an O. The father passes on either A or B. Children are therefore AO (type A) or BO (type B).
options: Correct. A or B, never AB or O.
A type O child needs an O copy from each parent; the AB father has none.
A type AB child needs an A from one parent and a B from the other; the mother can pass on only O.
O and AB are both impossible here.

why.correct: Agglutination is an immune process: antibodies bind antigens on several cells and cross-link them into clumps. Coagulation is thrombin converting fibrinogen into fibrin threads. They can happen together in a severe transfusion reaction, but they are different processes.
options: Platelets are central to clotting, not to agglutination.
Agglutination happens inside the vessels in a transfusion reaction as well as in a typing test.
Correct. Different molecules, different mechanisms.
They involve different molecules and are triggered differently.

why.correct: Exposure at the first delivery sensitizes the mother, who makes anti-D over weeks. In the next Rh-positive pregnancy, her anti-D crosses to the fetus and destroys its red cells, causing anemia and, after birth, rising bilirubin and jaundice.
The damage comes from the recipient's antibodies attacking the donor's red cells. Donor antibodies are few in a unit of packed red cells and are diluted in the recipient's large plasma volume.
options: This step is right. It starts the reaction.
This step is right. Antibodies cross-link the cells.
This is the error. The recipient's antibodies, not the donor's, cause the reaction.
This step is right. Hemolysis follows agglutination.
This step is right. Hemoglobin spills into the urine.

why.correct: Clumping with anti-B shows the B antigen; no clumping with anti-A or anti-D shows no A and no D antigen. The type is B negative.
options: Type A cells would clump with anti-A, not anti-B.
An Rh-positive sample would also clump with anti-D.
Correct. B antigen only: B negative.
Type O cells would not clump with anti-B.

why.correct: Type B plasma holds anti-A, so the donor cells must lack the A antigen: type B or type O.
options: AB red cells carry the A antigen, which the patient's anti-A would attack.
A cells carry the A antigen.
Correct. B and O cells both lack the A antigen.
Only an AB recipient can take any ABO type.

why.correct: After the first exposure, the mother's blood holds many anti-Rh antibodies. In the second panel they cross into the fetal vessels and attach to the fetus's Rh-positive red cells.
options: Correct. The antibodies, made after the first exposure, cause the harm.
Fetal cells leaking into the mother cause the first exposure. The harm in the second pregnancy is done by antibodies moving the other way.
No break is needed in the second pregnancy; the antibodies cross an intact barrier.
The drawing shows antibodies, not maternal red cells, reaching the fetus.

why.correct: A type O mother has anti-A and anti-B from infancy, with no earlier exposure needed. Most cannot reach the fetus, but a type O mother makes some that can. They bind the type A baby's red cells, and the destroyed cells raise bilirubin. ABO disease is usually mild because fetal cells carry A and B only weakly.
options: She is Rh positive, so she makes no anti-D; Rh disease is not possible.
Correct. Mild ABO hemolytic disease, which can occur in a first pregnancy.
The baby is type A and would not attack its own cells; newborns also make little anti-B yet.
An Rh-positive mother does not make anti-D.

why.correct: Donor cells must not carry an antigen the recipient has, or will make, antibodies against. O negative cells suit anyone; B negative cells suit an AB negative patient, who has no anti-B and no D to meet; O positive cells suit a B positive patient.
options: Correct. O negative cells carry no A, B or D.
The D antigen would sensitize her, putting future pregnancies at risk.
Correct. B antigen is her own, and there is no D.
An O patient has anti-A and anti-B, which would attack AB red cells.
Correct. O cells carry no A or B, and she is already Rh positive.

why.correct: ABO and Rh are only two of more than 40 blood group systems. A crossmatch mixes the patient's plasma with the donor's red cells; agglutination would reveal antibodies against another antigen on those cells.
options: A type A donor has no anti-A; the concern is the recipient's plasma meeting the donor's cells.
A crossmatch tests compatibility, not hemoglobin.
Correct. It catches incompatibilities beyond ABO and Rh.
The unit's type is already known; a crossmatch looks for reactions, not type.
